title: Closure through a homogeneous equation
stem: Determine a basis and dimension of $W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x+2y-z=0\}$, and prove that it is a subspace.
solution: The zero vector satisfies the equation. If $u,v$ satisfy it, its left side evaluated at $au+bv$ is $a$ times the left side at $u$ plus $b$ times the left side at $v$, hence zero. This proves closure for arbitrary real scalars. Solving for $x$ gives $(-2y+z,y,z)=y(-2,1,0)+z(1,0,1)$. The two displayed vectors span every solution. In a zero combination, the second and third coordinates force the two coefficients to vanish, so they are independent. They form a basis and the dimension is two. The ambient space still has dimension three; it is the one independent homogeneous constraint that removes a freedom.

title: An affine plane is not a subspace
stem: For $H=\{(x,y,z):x+2y-z=3\}$, decide subspace status and describe all points relative to one base point.
solution: Zero fails the equation, so $H$ is not a vector subspace with ordinary operations. The point $x_0=(3,0,0)$ belongs to $H$. Subtracting this point from any solution gives a vector satisfying $x+2y-z=0$, and adding any such homogeneous solution to $x_0$ preserves the right side three. Therefore $H=(3,0,0)+\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,0),(1,0,1)\}$. It has affine dimension two. There is no basis of $H$ in the ordinary vector-space sense. Describing it using a point and two independent directions is the correct affine representation.

title: Scaling closure does not give addition closure
stem: Is $S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:xy=0\}$ a subspace? Determine its span and the dimension of that span.
solution: The set is the union of the two coordinate axes. It contains zero and is closed under scalar multiplication, since $(ax)(ay)=a^2xy=0$. But $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ belong to it while their sum $(1,1)$ does not. It is therefore not a subspace and has no vector-space dimension under these operations. Its span does contain both coordinate unit vectors and hence every $(x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1)$. Thus its span is the whole plane and has dimension two. One must distinguish the original nonlinear set from the subspace generated by it.

title: Modified operations with a shifted zero
stem: On $\mathbb R^2$ define $u\oplus v=u+v-c$ and $a\odot u=au+(1-a)c$, where $c=(1,2)$. Prove vector-space status and find the zero vector and a basis.
solution: The map $\phi(u)=u-c$ is a bijection to ordinary $\mathbb R^2$. It satisfies $\phi(u\oplus v)=u+v-2c=\phi(u)+\phi(v)$ and $\phi(a\odot u)=a(u-c)=a\phi(u)$. Hence the operations inherit every vector-space axiom. The zero vector is $c$, since $u\oplus c=u$. The additive inverse of $u$ is $2c-u$. A basis is the preimage of the ordinary unit basis: $c+e_1=(2,2)$ and $c+e_2=(1,3)$. A combination in the modified operations corresponds under $\phi$ to the same coefficient combination of $e_1,e_2$, so existence and uniqueness are immediate. Ordinary determinants of the unshifted displayed points do not test this modified structure.

title: A false scalar multiplication axiom
stem: Keep ordinary addition on $\mathbb R^2$, but define $a\star(x,y)=(ax,0)$. Which axiom fails, despite closure?
solution: Take $v=(0,1)$. The prescribed operation gives $1\star v=(0,0)$, whereas the scalar identity axiom demands $1\star v=v$. Thus the structure is not a vector space. A successful closure check does not repair a failed identity law. The subset $\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}$ does become an ordinary one-dimensional vector space under the restricted operations, but that is a smaller set and a different assertion from claiming that all of $\mathbb R^2$ works.

title: Three parameters with only two freedoms
stem: Find a basis and dimension of $W=\{(a+b,2a+2b,c):a,b,c\in\mathbb R\}$. Describe the coefficient ambiguity.
solution: The parameterization is $(a+b)(1,2,0)+c(0,0,1)$. The two generators are independent because their first and third coordinates isolate the coefficients. They span the set, so the dimension is two. Changing $(a,b,c)$ to $(a+t,b-t,c)$ leaves every output unchanged. This is a one-dimensional parameter ambiguity, not an additional output direction. The parameter map from $\mathbb R^3$ has kernel $\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,0)\}$ and image dimension two, in agreement with rank-nullity. Merely counting the letters $a,b,c$ would overcount the dimension.

title: The logarithmic vector space
stem: On positive real numbers use $u\oplus v=uv$ and $a\odot u=u^a$. Find a basis, the coordinates of $8$ relative to basis $(2)$, and the additive inverse of $8$.
solution: The logarithm is an operation-preserving bijection to the real line, so this is a one-dimensional real vector space. Any positive number other than one can be a basis vector because its logarithm is nonzero. In particular, every $u>0$ is uniquely $2^c$ with $c=\log u/\log2$. The coordinates of eight are therefore $(3)$. The zero vector is one, and the additive inverse of eight is $1/8$, since $8\oplus(1/8)=1$. The ordinary number minus eight is not an admissible vector. These conclusions use the supplied operations, not ordinary addition.

title: A homogeneous-looking nonlinear restriction
stem: Let $W=\{p\in P_2(\mathbb R):p(0)p(1)=0\}$. Decide subspace status and find $\operatorname{span}W$.
solution: The polynomials $p=x$ and $q=1-x$ each satisfy the product condition. Their sum is one, for which the product of values at zero and one equals one, not zero. Hence addition fails. Nevertheless $x$, $1-x$, and $x^2$ belong to $W$. The first two generate one and $x$, while $x^2$ supplies the remaining monomial direction. Thus the span is $P_2$, dimension three. The condition is nonlinear in the unknown polynomial even though its right side is zero. Homogeneity under scaling is not sufficient for linearity.

title: Dependent linear constraints
stem: Find the dimension and a basis of the solutions in $\mathbb R^4$ of $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=0$, $2x_1+2x_2+2x_3+2x_4=0$, and $x_1-x_2=0$.
solution: The second equation is twice the first and adds no restriction. The third gives $x_2=x_1=t$. Set $x_3=s$; the first gives $x_4=-2t-s$. Thus the solution vector is $t(1,1,0,-2)+s(0,0,1,-1)$. The first and third coordinates force both coefficients in a zero combination to vanish, so these vectors are a basis. The dimension is two. The constraint matrix has rank two, giving $4-2=2$, rather than $4-3=1$. Both methods check the independence of restrictions.

title: A field restriction changes subspace status
stem: Is $W=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z=0\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb C$ over $\mathbb R$? Is it a subspace over $\mathbb C$?
solution: Over the reals, $W$ is the real axis. It is nonempty, sums of real numbers remain real, and real scalar multiples remain real. It has real basis $(1)$ and dimension one. Over the complex field, the scalar $i$ applied to the vector one gives $i$, which is outside $W$, so scalar closure fails. This does not contradict the real result: the set of allowed scalars changed. The ambient space itself has real dimension two and complex dimension one.

title: A dependency certificate from the original columns
stem: For $v_1=(1,0)$, $v_2=(0,1)$, and $v_3=(2,3)$, find all coefficient triples producing $(5,7)$ and extract a basis.
solution: The equations are $c_1+2c_3=5$ and $c_2+3c_3=7$. Letting $c_3=t$ gives $(c_1,c_2,c_3)=(5-2t,7-3t,t)$. Their difference direction $(-2,-3,1)$ is a nonzero kernel vector, reflecting $v_3=2v_1+3v_2$. The first two vectors are a basis of the whole plane. The target is one fixed vector, while its coefficients in the redundant three-vector generating list are not unique. In the extracted ordered basis $(v_1,v_2)$ its coordinates are uniquely $(5,7)$.

title: Joint independence versus pairwise tests
stem: Three nonzero vectors in $\mathbb R^2$ are pairwise nonparallel. Can they be independent? Give a certificate and explain the general bound.
solution: They cannot be independent because the ambient dimension is two. The concrete list $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ satisfies a relation with coefficients $(1,1,-1)$, although no pair is parallel. Any $2\times3$ column matrix has at most two pivots and therefore at least one free coefficient in its homogeneous system. That free coefficient produces a dependence. Pairwise nonparallelity only establishes independence of each pair, not of the full list.

title: Every vector need not be removable
stem: For the dependent list $(e_1,e_2,2e_2)$ in $\mathbb R^2$, determine which members can be removed without changing the span.
solution: The relation $2e_2-(2e_2)=0$ uses only the second and third list positions, so either of those positions can be removed. The remaining $e_1$ and nonzero vertical vector still span the plane. Removing $e_1$ leaves only vertical vectors and reduces the span to a line. Dependence guarantees at least one removable member, not that every member is removable. In a particular dependence relation, only positions with a nonzero coefficient can be solved for using that relation.

title: Independence of parameterized columns
stem: Classify the span of $(1,t)$ and $(t,1)$ over $\mathbb R$ for every real $t$.
solution: Their determinant is $1-t^2$. If $t\ne1,-1$, it is nonzero, and the vectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^2$. At $t=1$, both vectors equal $(1,1)$ and the span is that line. At $t=-1$, the second vector is the negative of $(1,-1)$ and the span is that line. Each exceptional case has dimension one because the first coordinate of the first vector is always one. It is incorrect to conclude that a zero determinant makes the span zero; it makes a two-vector basis of the plane impossible.

title: A rank jump that a generic simplification hides
stem: For $v_1=(1,0,1)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, and $v_3=(a,b,1)$, determine dependence and the dimension for all $a,b$.
solution: The first two vectors are independent. Their general combination is $(s,t,s+t)$, so the third belongs to their span exactly when $a+b=1$. In that case the dependence is $v_3-av_1-bv_2=0$, and the dimension is two. Otherwise the third lies outside the plane $z=x+y$, giving dimension three and a basis of $\mathbb R^3$. The determinant of their column matrix is $1-a-b$, confirming the classification. No parameter choice reduces the dimension below two because the fixed first two columns remain independent.

title: Transformed lists and a coefficient matrix
stem: Suppose $u,v,w$ are independent over $\mathbb R$. Are $u+v$, $v+w$, and $w+u$ independent? What changes in characteristic two?
solution: Relative to $(u,v,w)$, the new columns are $(1,1,0)^T,(0,1,1)^T,(1,0,1)^T$. Their determinant is two, so over the reals the new list is independent and is a basis of the original three-dimensional span. More directly, a zero relation gives $a+c=0$, $a+b=0$, and $b+c=0$, hence $2a=0$ and all coefficients vanish over the reals. In characteristic two, summing the three new vectors gives $2u+2v+2w=0$ with nonzero coefficients all one. Their rank is two because the first two are still independent. The field qualification is essential.

title: A span equality with explicit recovery
stem: For arbitrary vectors $u,v$, prove $\operatorname{span}(u,v)=\operatorname{span}(u+v,u-v)$ over $\mathbb R$, and determine whether the statement holds over $\mathbb F_2$.
solution: The two new vectors are combinations of the original ones, so the new span is contained in the old span. Conversely $u=((u+v)+(u-v))/2$ and $v=((u+v)-(u-v))/2$, proving the reverse inclusion over the reals. No independence assumption on $u,v$ is needed for this span identity. Over $\mathbb F_2$, the two new vectors coincide because minus equals plus. If $u=e_1,v=e_2$, their original span is two-dimensional but the new span is a line. Division by two is exactly the invalid step in that field.

title: The exact relation space
stem: Let $v_1=(1,2,0)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, $v_3=(1,3,1)$, $v_4=(2,5,1)$. Find a basis of their span and every dependence coefficient vector.
solution: The identities $v_3=v_1+v_2$ and $v_4=2v_1+v_2$ show that the first two span the whole list. They are independent because their first and third coordinates separate coefficients, so the output dimension is two. A zero combination reduces to $(c_1+c_3+2c_4)v_1+(c_2+c_3+c_4)v_2=0$. Therefore set $c_3=s,c_4=t$, giving $c=(-s-2t,-s-t,s,t)$. The relation space has basis $(-1,-1,1,0)$ and $(-2,-1,0,1)$, also dimension two. Its coordinate length is four, whereas the output vectors have length three.

title: Function independence from evaluation
stem: Prove that $1$, $e^x$, and $e^{2x}$ are independent as real functions on $\mathbb R$.
solution: Suppose $a+be^x+ce^{2x}=0$ for every real $x$. Put $t=e^x$, which ranges over all positive real numbers. The polynomial $a+bt+ct^2$ has infinitely many roots, so it is the zero polynomial and $a=b=c=0$. Alternatively evaluate at $x=0,\log2,\log3$: the coefficient equations have Vandermonde determinant $(2-1)(3-1)(3-2)=2$, nonzero. Either method supplies a full identity argument. Cancellation at a single value of $x$ would not establish dependence or independence of functions.

title: A singular sample matrix is inconclusive
stem: The functions $1$ and $x^2$ give equal sample columns at nodes $-1,1$. Does that prove dependence? Resolve the issue completely.
solution: At the two stated nodes the columns are both $(1,1)^T$, so the sample matrix is singular. This means the chosen evaluation map loses information on their two-dimensional span. The polynomial identity $a+bx^2=0$ for every real $x$ instead gives $a=0$ at zero and then $b=0$ at one. Thus the functions are independent. A nonsingular evaluation matrix is a sufficient certificate of independence, but a singular one is not a sufficient certificate of dependence. The latter requires an actual nontrivial identity, not a failure of one selected sampling scheme.

title: Basis extraction from an echelon form
stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0&3\\2&4&1&4\\3&6&2&5\end{bmatrix}$, find bases of its column space, row space, and nullspace.
solution: Subtract twice row one from row two and three times row one from row three. The last two rows become $(0,0,1,-2)$ and $(0,0,2,-4)$. Subtract twice the new second row from the third. The resulting reduced matrix has nonzero rows $(1,2,0,3)$ and $(0,0,1,-2)$, which form a row-space basis. Pivot positions are columns one and three, so take the original columns $(1,2,3)^T,(0,1,2)^T$ for a column-space basis. The equations $x_1=-2x_2-3x_4$ and $x_3=2x_4$ give nullspace basis $(-2,1,0,0)^T,(-3,0,2,1)^T$. Multiplication by the original $A$ verifies both vanish. Rank two and nullity two sum to four.

title: Why reduced columns may answer the wrong question
stem: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$. Its reduced form has first column $(1,0)^T$. Is that a basis vector for $\operatorname{Col}A$?
solution: No. The original column space is the line $\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^T\}$. The vector $(1,0)^T$ is not on that line: matching its first coordinate forces scalar one, whose second coordinate would be two. Row operations preserve dependencies and pivot indices but transform the column space by an invertible left factor. The pivot index one correctly selects original column one, $(1,2)^T$. The reduced first column is a basis of the transformed column space, not the original one. Both spaces have dimension one, which does not make them equal.

title: Extending a prescribed independent list
stem: Extend $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$ to a basis of $\mathbb R^3$ using a standard unit vector, and prove the extension works.
solution: The first two vectors are independent because their first and third coordinates force coefficients to vanish. A general vector in their span is $(a,a+b,b)$, which satisfies $y=x+z$. The unit vector $e_1=(1,0,0)$ violates that equation, so it lies outside the span. Adding it therefore preserves independence. The three vectors form a basis of dimension-three space. Alternatively the determinant of the columns $(1,1,0),(0,1,1),e_1$ equals one. Selecting a nonzero vector alone would not suffice; it must lie outside the existing span.

title: An allowed exchange and a forbidden exchange
stem: Let $B=(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be the standard ordered basis of $\mathbb R^3$, and let $w=2e_1-e_2$. Which single members of $B$ can be replaced by $w$ while retaining a basis?
solution: The coefficients of $w$ in $B$ are $(2,-1,0)$. Replacing $e_1$ works because $e_1=(w+e_2)/2$. Replacing $e_2$ works because $e_2=2e_1-w$. In either case the old basis can be recovered, so the replacement spans and has three vectors, hence is a basis. Replacing $e_3$ fails because all remaining vectors lie in the plane $z=0$. The exchange theorem permits replacement at nonzero coefficient positions, not arbitrary positions. Over characteristic two the coefficient on $e_1$ vanishes, so that exchange must be reconsidered.

title: A dimension bound is not a spanning certificate
stem: A list contains four vectors in a four-dimensional space. Must it be a basis? State two sufficient additional conditions and a counterexample.
solution: The number alone is insufficient. The list $(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_1+e_2)$ has four members but spans only the first three coordinate directions and is dependent. If the four vectors are known independent, the dimension theorem makes them a basis. If they are known to span, the same theorem forces independence and they are a basis. The premise must be one of these actual structural properties; the count four only allows the other property to be inferred after one has been verified.

title: A maximal list relative to a candidate set
stem: In $\mathbb R^3$, the list $e_1,e_2$ is maximal independent among candidates $e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2$. Is it a basis of the ambient space?
solution: It is a basis of the candidates' span, namely the plane $z=0$. It is not maximal independent in all of $\mathbb R^3$, because $e_3$ can be added. Thus it is not an ambient basis. Maximality always refers to a specified universe of allowable added vectors. The theorem saying maximal independent sets are bases uses maximality in the whole vector space being spanned. A greedy algorithm restricted to a supplied generator list returns a basis of that list's span; it does not create missing ambient directions.

title: Nonunique representation count over a finite field
stem: Over $\mathbb F_3$, a $4\times7$ matrix has rank three. How many coefficient vectors solve $Ac=b$ when the system is consistent? How many right sides are attainable?
solution: Nullity is $7-3=4$. A four-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_3$ has $3^4=81$ vectors. Every consistent solution set is one translate of this kernel, so has exactly 81 coefficient vectors. The column space has dimension three and contains $3^3=27$ attainable right sides among all $3^4=81$ possible four-coordinate outputs. An inconsistent right side has no solutions. Infinitely many solutions is a real-field conclusion, not a conclusion that follows from positive nullity over every field.

title: A nested dimension chain
stem: Let $U\subsetneq W\subsetneq V$, where $\dim V=7$ and $\dim U=5$. Determine $\dim W$ and describe an adapted basis.
solution: In finite dimension, a proper inclusion of subspaces forces a strict increase in dimension. Therefore $5<\dim W<7$, giving $\dim W=6$. Choose a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_5$ of $U$. Since $W$ is larger, select $w\in W\setminus U$; adjoining it gives six independent vectors, hence a basis of $W$. Select $v\in V\setminus W$; the seven-vector list is a basis of $V$. This construction makes both inclusions visible and proves that no alternative integer dimension is possible.

title: Equal dimensions without inclusion
stem: Two subspaces of $\mathbb R^3$ have dimension two. Must they be equal? Give a counterexample and an exact additional hypothesis that would suffice.
solution: The planes $U=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$ and $W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_3)$ both have dimension two but differ because $e_2\in U$ and $e_2\notin W$. If $U\subseteq W$ is additionally known, a basis of $U$ has two independent vectors in the two-dimensional space $W$, so it spans $W$ and the spaces are equal. Equality of dimensions by itself compares sizes of bases, not positions of subspaces in the ambient space.

title: Coordinates in a nonstandard basis
stem: For $B=((1,1),(1,-1))$, find $[(3,1)]_B$ and the coordinates of the same vector in $C=((2,0),(1,1))$.
solution: In basis $B$, the equations $a+b=3$ and $a-b=1$ give $a=2,b=1$. Hence $[(3,1)]_B=(2,1)^T$. In basis $C$, the second coordinate of the original vector gives coefficient $d=1$ on $(1,1)$, and $2c+d=3$ gives $c=1$. Thus its $C$ coordinates are $(1,1)^T$. Reconstructing gives $2(1,1)+(1,-1)=(3,1)$ and $(2,0)+(1,1)=(3,1)$. The vector is unchanged while coordinate numbers differ.

title: Change-of-basis direction
stem: For the bases $B,C$ in Question 30, compute $P_{C\leftarrow B}$ and use it to convert $(2,1)^T$.
solution: The first vector of $B$ equals the second vector of $C$, so its $C$ coordinates are $(0,1)^T$. The second vector $(1,-1)$ has $C$ coordinates $(1,-1)^T$, since $(2,0)-(1,1)=(1,-1)$. Place these as columns to obtain $P_{C\leftarrow B}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$. Multiplying by $(2,1)^T$ yields $(1,1)^T$, as expected. The reverse matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, which sends $(1,1)^T$ back to $(2,1)^T$. Basis-vector coordinates belong in columns, and the arrow determines which basis supplies the input coordinates.

title: Coordinates in a proper subspace
stem: Let $B=((1,0,1),(0,1,1))$. Find coordinates of $(2,3,5)$ in this basis of its span, and explain why an ordinary inverse of the basis matrix is unavailable.
solution: A combination is $(a,b,a+b)$, so the target has unique coefficients $a=2,b=3$. The third coordinate checks consistency: $5=2+3$. Thus the coordinates are $(2,3)^T$. The basis matrix is $3\times2$, so it has no two-sided ordinary matrix inverse. Its columns are independent and coordinate recovery on its image is unique, but not every vector of $\mathbb R^3$ lies in that image. For example, $(2,3,6)$ is inconsistent. One can solve the rectangular system or choose a suitable left inverse; writing the square-inverse formula without checking shape is invalid.

title: Dual coordinates as rows of the inverse
stem: For $B=((1,1),(1,-1))$, find the two dual basis functionals and evaluate them on $(5,-3)$.
solution: The basis matrix is $S=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ with inverse $S^{-1}=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$. Its rows give $\ell_1(x,y)=(x+y)/2$ and $\ell_2(x,y)=(x-y)/2$. Direct evaluation gives $\ell_i(b_j)=\delta_{ij}$, establishing the dual property. On $(5,-3)$ the values are one and four, so $(5,-3)=1(1,1)+4(1,-1)$. These are linear functionals reading coefficients; calling the original basis orthonormal would be wrong because its vectors have squared length two rather than one.

title: A polynomial basis with a triangular coefficient matrix
stem: Show that $(1,1+x,1+x+x^2)$ is a basis of $P_2(\mathbb R)$ and find coordinates of $2+3x+4x^2$.
solution: Its coefficient matrix relative to $(1,x,x^2)$ is upper triangular with unit diagonal, hence determinant one and independent columns. As $P_2$ has dimension three, this list is a basis. Write $a+b(1+x)+c(1+x+x^2)=2+3x+4x^2$. Comparing the quadratic coefficient gives $c=4$; comparing the linear coefficient gives $b+c=3$, so $b=-1$; comparing the constant coefficient gives $a+b+c=2$, so $a=-1$. Coordinates are $(-1,-1,4)^T$. Substitution reconstructs the polynomial exactly. The coefficients in a nonmonomial basis are not simply its monomial coefficients.

title: Distinct roots remove independent freedoms
stem: Find a basis of $W=\{p\in P_4(\mathbb R):p(0)=p(1)=p(2)=0\}$.
solution: Each polynomial is divisible by $r(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)$ because the three roots are distinct. Since the degree is at most four, the quotient has degree at most one. Thus $p=(a+bx)r(x)$, and a basis is $(r,xr)$. They are independent because a zero combination implies $(a+bx)r=0$ as a polynomial and the nonzero polynomial $r$ cannot annihilate a nonzero polynomial factor. The dimension is two, matching $5-3$. The root count applies to distinct nodes; writing a repeated copy of one evaluation condition would not remove a further freedom.

title: Repeated roots and derivative conditions
stem: Find a basis of the polynomials in $P_4(\mathbb R)$ satisfying $p(1)=p'(1)=0$ and $p(-1)=0$.
solution: The first two conditions make one a root of multiplicity at least two, while the last makes minus one a root. Therefore $p$ is divisible by $r(x)=(x-1)^2(x+1)$ of degree three. The allowed quotient is $a+bx$, so $(r,xr)$ is a basis and the dimension is two. The conditions are independent here: divisibility gives exactly three degrees of restriction in a five-dimensional space. Differentiation and multiplicity are being used over the reals; in positive characteristic, one must verify derivative behavior rather than assume every real argument transfers unchanged.

title: Dependent evaluation equations
stem: In $P_3(\mathbb R)$ impose $p(0)=0$, $p(1)=0$, and $p(0)+2p(1)=0$. Find dimension and basis.
solution: The third condition follows from the first two, so there are only two independent evaluation constraints. Every admissible polynomial is divisible by $x(x-1)$ and has a quotient of degree at most one. Hence $(x(x-1),x^2(x-1))$ is a basis and the dimension is two. The two basis vectors have distinct degrees and are nonzero, proving independence by comparing leading coefficients. Subtracting three from the ambient dimension four would be wrong because the functional restrictions have rank two.

title: A nonhomogeneous interpolation fiber
stem: Describe all $p\in P_3(\mathbb R)$ with $p(0)=1$ and $p(1)=2$, and state whether the solution set is a subspace.
solution: The polynomial $p_0=1+x$ meets both data. The difference $p-p_0$ must vanish at zero and one, so $p=1+x+(a+bx)x(x-1)$. Conversely every such polynomial satisfies the two evaluations. The set is an affine translate of a two-dimensional homogeneous kernel. It is not a subspace because zero fails $p(0)=1$. The two directions $x(x-1)$ and $x^2(x-1)$ describe variation between solutions, but are not a basis of the affine set itself under ordinary operations.

title: Integral and derivative constraints
stem: Find a basis of $W\subseteq P_3(\mathbb R)$ defined by $\int_0^1p(x)\,dx=0$ and $p'(0)=0$.
solution: Write $p=a+bx+cx^2+dx^3$. The derivative condition gives $b=0$. The integral becomes $a+c/3+d/4=0$, so $a=-c/3-d/4$. Thus $p=c(x^2-1/3)+d(x^3-1/4)$, and those two polynomials form a basis. Their quadratic and cubic coefficients isolate the two parameters in a zero combination. Both constraints are homogeneous linear functionals and independent: the derivative reads $b$, while the integral has a nonzero coefficient on $a$. The dimension is $4-2=2$, not a count inferred merely from the appearance of calculus notation.

title: All polynomials versus finite-support sequences
stem: Prove that the monomials form a basis of $\mathbb R[x]$, but the coordinate unit sequences do not span all real sequences.
solution: Every polynomial is, by definition, a finite sum of monomials with unique coefficients. Comparing coefficients shows independence of every finite monomial sublist, so the full monomial set is an algebraic basis. For sequences, a finite combination of coordinate unit sequences has only finitely many nonzero entries. The sequence $(1,1,1,\ldots)$ has infinitely many nonzero entries and cannot be such a combination. The unit sequences are independent but span only finite-support sequences. An infinite series of unit sequences is not allowed by the algebraic span definition; adding convergence structure would be a separate problem.

title: Symmetric matrices with zero trace
origin: Original generalization of MSc CS 1405 Q41
stem: Over $\mathbb R$, find a basis and dimension of symmetric $n\times n$ matrices with trace zero, for $n\ge1$.
solution: Choose the off-diagonal basis matrices $E_{ij}+E_{ji}$ for $i<j$, and diagonal matrices $E_{ii}-E_{nn}$ for $i<n$. Any symmetric matrix has independent upper-triangular entries, and trace zero determines its last diagonal entry as the negative sum of the others. Therefore the displayed list spans. Looking at each upper-triangular entry first forces all off-diagonal coefficients in a zero combination to vanish; then diagonal positions $i<n$ force the remaining coefficients to vanish. The dimension is $n(n-1)/2+n-1=n(n+1)/2-1$. At $n=1$, the space is zero and the basis is empty. At $n=4$, the formula yields nine, matching the authentic item.

title: Symmetric and skew-symmetric decomposition
stem: Prove $M_n(\mathbb R)=S\oplus K$, where $S$ is symmetric and $K$ skew-symmetric. Explain why the analogous assertion fails in characteristic two for $n\ge1$.
solution: Every matrix decomposes as $(A+A^T)/2+(A-A^T)/2$. Transposing shows the first term is symmetric and the second skew-symmetric. If a matrix belongs to both, it satisfies $A=-A$, hence $2A=0$ and $A=0$ over the reals. This gives spanning and uniqueness, so the sum is direct. Their dimensions $n(n+1)/2$ and $n(n-1)/2$ add to $n^2$. In characteristic two, $-A=A$, so the equations defining $S$ and $K$ coincide; the identity matrix lies in both. Also division by two is unavailable. The directness claim therefore fails, including the $n=1$ case under the literal definition $A^T=-A$.

title: Two matrix constraints with a dependency
stem: Find the dimension of $3\times3$ real matrices whose every row sum and every column sum is zero, and give a basis construction.
solution: Choose the top-left $2\times2$ entries freely. Zero row sums determine the third entry in each of the first two rows; zero column sums determine the first two entries of the last row. The remaining corner must equal the sum of the four chosen entries, which satisfies both its row and column equations. Thus there are four independent freedoms. A basis is $E_{ij}-E_{i3}-E_{3j}+E_{33}$ for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$. Each has zero row and column sums, and the four top-left entries isolate its coefficients. Of the six written constraints, one is dependent because total row sum equals total column sum; their rank is five.

title: Symmetry plus row sums
stem: Find the dimension and a constructive description of symmetric real $4\times4$ matrices satisfying $A\mathbf1=0$.
solution: Choose the six entries strictly above the diagonal arbitrarily and reflect them below. Each row-sum condition then uniquely determines its diagonal entry as the negative sum of the off-diagonal entries in that row. These four equations are independent on the symmetric space because each reads a separate diagonal coordinate. Thus dimension is $10-4=6$. A basis uses one chosen pair $i<j$: put one in positions $(i,j),(j,i)$ and minus one in diagonal positions $(i,i),(j,j)$. All other entries are zero. The six off-diagonal positions isolate coefficients and prove independence. No extra dependency among row sums arises here merely from symmetry.

title: Commuting with a diagonal matrix
stem: Let $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2,3)$. Find the dimension and a basis of real matrices $A$ satisfying $AD=DA$.
solution: The $(i,j)$ entry equation is $a_{ij}d_j=d_i a_{ij}$, or $(d_j-d_i)a_{ij}=0$. An entry is free exactly when the two diagonal values coincide. The repeated value one gives a free $2\times2$ upper-left block, while the singleton values two and three give one diagonal entry each. All entries between different blocks must vanish. Thus the dimension is $2^2+1^2+1^2=6$. The six allowed elementary matrices $E_{11},E_{12},E_{21},E_{22},E_{33},E_{44}$ form a basis. The commutation equation is homogeneous linear in $A$, despite involving multiplication by a fixed matrix.

title: A nonlinear matrix set and its linear span
stem: Do the singular real $2\times2$ matrices form a subspace? Determine their linear span.
solution: The matrices $E_{11}$ and $E_{22}$ are singular, but their sum is the identity and is invertible. Therefore addition closure fails. Every elementary matrix $E_{ij}$ is singular in order two, and the four elementary matrices form a basis of $M_2(\mathbb R)$. Hence the singular matrices span the whole four-dimensional matrix space. The original singular set has no vector-space dimension under inherited operations; four is the dimension of its span. The order-one boundary differs: the only singular $1\times1$ matrix is zero, which is a subspace.

title: Polynomial parity and a direct sum
stem: Decompose $P_5(\mathbb R)$ into even and odd polynomial subspaces. Find dimensions and the components of $2+3x-4x^2+x^5$.
solution: The even subspace has basis $(1,x^2,x^4)$, dimension three, and the odd subspace has basis $(x,x^3,x^5)$, also dimension three. Their intersection is zero because a polynomial satisfying $p(-x)=p(x)$ and $p(-x)=-p(x)$ must be zero over the reals. Their basis lists concatenate to the full monomial basis, proving the direct sum. The even component is $2-4x^2$ and the odd component is $3x+x^5$. They can also be obtained from $(p(x)+p(-x))/2$ and $(p(x)-p(-x))/2$. This argument again relies on characteristic not two.

title: A sum and intersection from explicit planes
stem: Let $U=\{(x,y,z):z=0\}$ and $W=\{(x,y,z):y=0\}$. Find bases of $U\cap W$ and $U+W$, and all decompositions of $(a,b,c)$ as $u+w$.
solution: The intersection satisfies both $y=z=0$, so its basis is $(e_1)$ and dimension one. The sum contains $e_1,e_2,e_3$, so it is the whole space. A decomposition has $u=(t,b,0)$ and $w=(a-t,0,c)$ for any real $t$. This is every possible decomposition: the second coordinate can come only from $U$, the third only from $W$, and the first is shared. Nonuniqueness is exactly the freedom along the intersection. Dimension confirms $3=2+2-1$. This is a sum, but not a direct sum.

title: Intersecting two equation-defined spaces
stem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ satisfy $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=0$, and let $W$ satisfy $x_1=x_2$, $x_3=x_4$. Find all relevant dimensions and an intersection basis.
solution: The first space has one independent restriction, so dimension three. A vector in $W$ is $(a,a,b,b)$, giving dimension two. In the intersection, $2a+2b=0$, so over the reals $b=-a$. Its basis is $(1,1,-1,-1)$ and dimension one. The sum dimension is $3+2-1=4$, hence the whole ambient space. Directness fails because the intersection is nonzero. The calculation $2a+2b=0\Rightarrow a+b=0$ uses the real field; in characteristic two the entire $W$ would lie in $U$, changing the dimensions of intersection and sum.

title: Intersection through generator coordinates
stem: Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1,0),(0,1,0,1)\}$ and $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0,0),(0,0,1,1)\}$. Find an intersection basis and a sum basis.
solution: Equate $(a,b,a,b)$ from $U$ with $(c,c,d,d)$ from $W$. Coordinate comparison gives $a=b=c=d$, so the intersection is generated by $(1,1,1,1)$. Each original list is independent and has dimension two; the sum therefore has dimension three. A sum basis is the two $U$ generators together with $(1,1,0,0)$ from $W$. The latter is outside $U$ because its first and third coordinates differ. The omitted fourth generator equals the sum of the two $U$ generators minus the chosen $W$ generator, so spanning is explicitly verified.

title: Redundant generators inflate a block nullspace
stem: Take $B_U=[e_1\ e_1]$ and $B_W=[e_1]$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Compare the nullity of $[B_U\ -B_W]$ with $\dim(U\cap W)$.
solution: Both spans are the same one-dimensional line, so the intersection dimension is one. The block matrix has columns $e_1,e_1,-e_1$ and rank one, hence nullity two. Its coefficient equation is $a_1+a_2-b=0$. The solution $(1,-1,0)$ maps under $B_Ua$ to zero, describing only redundancy in $B_U$. The solution $(1,0,1)$ maps to $e_1$ and supplies the actual intersection direction. Thus block nullspace vectors must be mapped to actual output vectors, and zero or dependent outputs removed when the supplied lists are not bases. Equating nullity with intersection dimension requires independent lists on both sides.

title: Sharp intersection bounds
stem: Two subspaces of a ten-dimensional real space each have dimension six. Determine every possible intersection dimension and construct examples.
solution: The lower bound is $6+6-10=2$, and the intersection cannot exceed either dimension, giving integers $k=2,3,4,5,6$. Fix $U=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_6)$. For each such $k$, let $W$ be generated by $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ and $e_7,\ldots,e_{12-k}$. There are $k+(6-k)=6$ independent coordinate directions in $W$, and the largest index is at most ten because $k\ge2$. Exactly the first $k$ directions are shared, so the intersection has dimension $k$. This shows every value in the bound is attainable, not merely allowed by an inequality.

title: Forced nonzero intersection
stem: Let $V$ be finite-dimensional. If $U,W\subseteq V$ are subspaces and both dimensions exceed $\dim V/2$, prove that the intersection contains a nonzero vector. Does equality suffice?
solution: Let $n=\dim V$ be finite. The dimension formula gives $\dim(U\cap W)\ge\dim U+\dim W-n$. Under the strict hypotheses this is a positive integer, so the intersection is nonzero. Equality in both half-dimension bounds does not suffice: in $\mathbb R^4$, the spaces generated by $e_1,e_2$ and by $e_3,e_4$ each have dimension two and intersect only at zero. The strict inequality is doing actual work. For odd $n$, integer dimensions can strengthen a numerical lower bound, but the same sum-of-dimensions criterion governs the result.

title: Two-subspace union theorem
stem: Prove that the union of two subspaces is a subspace exactly when one contains the other.
solution: If one contains the other, the union is just the larger subspace. Conversely suppose neither contains the other. Choose $u\in U\setminus W$ and $w\in W\setminus U$. If $u+w$ belonged to $U$, subtracting $u$ would put $w$ in $U$, contradiction. If it belonged to $W$, subtracting $w$ would put $u$ in $W$, also a contradiction. Thus the union fails addition. The proof uses only additive subgroup properties and works over every field. It is a theorem about two subspaces; finite unions of three or more can behave differently over finite fields.

title: Three pairwise-trivial intersections are insufficient
stem: Let $U_1=\operatorname{span}e_1$, $U_2=\operatorname{span}e_2$, and $U_3=\operatorname{span}(e_1+e_2)$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Are their sum and pairwise intersections enough to establish directness?
solution: Each pair of distinct lines intersects only at zero, and the first two already span the plane. However $e_1+e_2+(-(e_1+e_2))=0$ gives nonzero components from all three spaces. Therefore the three-space sum is not direct. Its dimension is two while the sum of component dimensions is three. The correct sequential check fails at $U_3\cap(U_1+U_2)=U_3$, not zero. Pairwise intersection tests miss relations involving more than two components.

title: A nonorthogonal complement
stem: Let $U=\operatorname{span}(1,0)$ and $W=\operatorname{span}(1,2)$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Prove they are complements and find the decomposition of $(5,6)$.
solution: The two generating columns have determinant two, so they are independent and span the plane. Therefore the sum is direct. Solving $(5,6)=a(1,0)+b(1,2)$ gives $2b=6$, so $b=3$, and $a+b=5$, so $a=2$. The components are $(2,0)$ and $(3,6)$. They are not perpendicular: the dot product of the generating vectors is one. A direct sum is an algebraic uniqueness statement, not an assertion of right angles. Every other nonhorizontal line also complements this $U$.

title: The dimension formula does not extend by naïve inclusion-exclusion
stem: Does $\dim(U+W+Z)$ always equal the sum of individual dimensions minus pairwise intersection dimensions plus the triple-intersection dimension?
solution: No. Use the three distinct lines in Question 55. Each individual dimension is one, all pairwise intersection dimensions are zero, and the triple intersection is zero. The proposed expression gives three, but their sum is the plane of dimension two. The valid iterative formula is $\dim(U+W+Z)=\dim(U+W)+\dim Z-\dim((U+W)\cap Z)$. In this example the final intersection is the entire line $Z$, of dimension one, so the result is $2+1-1=2$. The failure comes from relations across three components that pairwise intersections do not encode.

title: Polynomial intersections and least common multiples
stem: In $P_5(\mathbb R)$, let $U$ contain multiples of $x(x-1)$ and $W$ contain multiples of $(x-1)(x-2)$. Find dimensions of both, their intersection, and their sum.
solution: Each required factor has degree two, so each space has quotient freedom $P_3$ and dimension four. A polynomial in both is divisible by the least common multiple $x(x-1)(x-2)$, not by the product with the repeated factor squared. Its quotient has degree at most two, so intersection dimension is three. The sum dimension is $4+4-3=5$. Both spaces vanish at one, so their sum is contained in the five-dimensional space of polynomials in $P_5$ vanishing at one. Equality follows from inclusion and equal finite dimension. This identifies the sum rather than merely counting it.

title: A quotient basis from an adapted basis
stem: Let $V=\mathbb R^3$ and $U=\operatorname{span}(1,1,0)$. Find a basis of $V/U$ and coordinates of the coset $(2,3,4)+U$ in it.
solution: The list $(1,1,0),e_2,e_3$ is a basis of $V$: its determinant is one. Therefore the cosets $e_2+U,e_3+U$ form a quotient basis. Write $(2,3,4)=2(1,1,0)+1e_2+4e_3$. The component in $U$ vanishes in the quotient, leaving coordinates $(1,4)^T$. Any other representative obtained by adding $t(1,1,0)$ has second minus first coordinate still one and third coordinate still four, so the quotient coordinates are well-defined. The quotient has dimension two; its vectors are cosets, not two particular real coordinates until a basis is chosen.

title: The quotient is not set subtraction
stem: For the horizontal axis $U$ in $\mathbb R^2$, identify the zero of $\mathbb R^2/U$ and decide whether $(1,2)+U$ and $(7,2)+U$ are distinct.
solution: The quotient zero is the coset $U$ itself, the entire horizontal axis. The difference $(1,2)-(7,2)=(-6,0)$ lies in $U$, so the two cosets are equal. Both are the horizontal line at height two. The quotient remembers height and ignores horizontal displacement, making it one-dimensional. The set difference $\mathbb R^2\setminus U$ is unrelated: it excludes every point of the zero coset and is not the quotient vector set. Representatives are individual points; quotient vectors are whole equivalence classes of those points.

title: An annihilator with explicit equations
stem: For $U=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, find all linear functionals vanishing on $U$.
solution: Write a functional as $\ell(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz$. Vanishing on the two generators gives $a+b=0$ and $b+c=0$, hence $(a,b,c)=t(1,-1,1)$. Thus the annihilator has basis $\ell_0(x,y,z)=x-y+z$ and dimension one. The underlying subspace is the plane $x-y+z=0$, of dimension two, so annihilator dimension is $3-2=1$. Every functional in this one-dimensional family vanishes on every combination of the generators by linearity, not merely at the two listed points.

title: Restriction of scalars
stem: If $V$ has complex dimension three, prove its real dimension is six and construct a real basis from a complex basis $v_1,v_2,v_3$.
solution: Take the six real vectors $v_1,iv_1,v_2,iv_2,v_3,iv_3$. Every complex coefficient is $a_j+ib_j$ with real parts, so every vector of $V$ is a real combination of these six, proving spanning. If a real combination vanishes, group it as $\sum_j(a_j+ib_j)v_j=0$. Complex independence gives $a_j+ib_j=0$ for each $j$, so every real coefficient vanishes. They are independent and hence a real basis. Complex independence does not mean the original three vectors alone span $V$ using only real coefficients; scalar freedom has changed.

title: Counting ordered bases
stem: How many ordered bases does $\mathbb F_2^3$ have? How many unordered bases?
solution: The first vector can be any of seven nonzero vectors. Its line contains two vectors including zero, so the second has $8-2=6$ choices. Two independent vectors span a plane of four elements, so the third has $8-4=4$ choices. The number of ordered bases is $7\cdot6\cdot4=168$. Every unordered basis has three distinct members and exactly $3!=6$ orderings, so the number of unordered bases is 28. Dividing by a factorial is justified only after confirming the elements are distinct and every order is counted equally; independence guarantees that here.

title: Three proper finite-field subspaces can cover
stem: List the three one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb F_2^2$ and show that their union is the whole space.
solution: The four vectors are $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$. Each nonzero vector generates a line containing just itself and zero, because the only scalars are zero and one. Therefore the three lines are $\{0,(1,0)\}$, $\{0,(0,1)\}$, and $\{0,(1,1)\}$. Their union contains all four vectors. Every line is proper and no one contains another, yet the union of all three is a subspace, namely the ambient space. This does not violate the two-subspace union theorem, which cannot be applied by assuming the union of the first two is already a subspace.

title: Formal polynomial versus polynomial function
stem: Over $\mathbb F_3$, does the nonzero formal polynomial $x^3-x$ represent a nonzero function on the field? What happens to evaluation on $P_3(\mathbb F_3)$?
solution: At zero, one, and two, the values of $x^3-x$ are zero modulo three. Its formal coefficients are not all zero, so it is a nonzero polynomial representing the zero function on the three-element domain. The evaluation map from the four-dimensional formal space $P_3$ to three-coordinate value lists therefore has a nontrivial kernel. In fact every value tuple is attainable by a degree-at-most-two interpolation polynomial, so the map has rank three and nullity one, generated by $x^3-x$. Independence of formal monomials does not imply independence of their induced functions on a finite domain.

title: A proper subspace with equal infinite dimension
stem: Compare the bases of $\mathbb R[x]$ and $x\mathbb R[x]$. Does equal basis cardinality force these spaces equal?
solution: The first has basis $(1,x,x^2,\ldots)$ and the second $(x,x^2,x^3,\ldots)$. Both are countably infinite lists, and each is independent and spans its stated space by finite coefficient expansions. The second space is proper because it contains no polynomial with a nonzero constant term, in particular not one. Thus equal infinite basis cardinality and inclusion do not force equality. The finite-dimensional proof of equality would add one new independent vector and contradict a fixed finite bound; countably many vectors plus one is still countably many, so that argument no longer yields a contradiction.

title: A parameterized intersection
stem: Let $U=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$ and $W_t=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,t),(0,1,t)\}$ in $\mathbb R^3$. Classify $U\cap W_t$ and $U+W_t$ for all real $t$.
solution: The generators of $W_t$ are independent for every $t$ because their first two coordinates are unit vectors, so its dimension is always two. Its general vector is $(a,b,t(a+b))$. At $t=0$, $W_t=U$, so intersection and sum both have dimension two. For $t\ne0$, being in $U$ requires $a+b=0$, giving intersection basis $(1,-1,0)$. The sum dimension is then $2+2-1=3$ and it equals $\mathbb R^3$. Dividing by $t$ before isolating zero would incorrectly discard the larger-intersection case.

title: Minimum constraints needed to specify a space
stem: A subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb R^7$ has dimension four. What is the minimum number of scalar homogeneous linear equations whose common solution set is $W$? Prove attainability.
solution: Any constraint matrix with kernel $W$ must have rank $7-4=3$, so at least three scalar equations are necessary. To construct three, extend a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_4$ of $W$ to a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_7$ of the ambient space. The last three coordinate-reading functionals in this basis vanish exactly when the added three coordinates are zero. Their common kernel is $W$, and they are independent because each reads a different added basis vector. Thus three equations are both necessary and sufficient. More equations can describe the same space, but must then include dependencies.

title: A finite-function space and constrained values
stem: Let $X$ have five elements. Find the dimension of the real functions on $X$ satisfying $\sum_{x\in X}f(x)=0$, and exhibit a basis.
solution: Label the points $x_1,\ldots,x_5$. The indicator functions $\delta_j$ taking one at $x_j$ and zero elsewhere form a basis of the full five-dimensional function space. The sum condition is a nonzero linear functional. A constrained basis is $\delta_1-\delta_5,\ldots,\delta_4-\delta_5$. A function with zero total is reconstructed from its first four values using these directions; its fifth value is their negative sum. Independence follows by evaluating at each of the first four points. The constrained dimension is four. The function set has infinitely many members over the reals, even though its domain and dimension are finite.

title: Dimension of a recurrence solution space
stem: Let $V$ be the real sequences satisfying $a_{n+2}=3a_{n+1}-2a_n$ for all $n\ge0$. Prove $\dim V=2$ and give a basis.
solution: The recurrence is homogeneous linear, so solutions form a subspace of all sequences. A solution is uniquely determined by its first two values: the recurrence computes every later term, and any initial pair is allowed. The initial-value map to $\mathbb R^2$ is therefore a linear bijection. Two explicit solutions are $u_n=1$ and $v_n=2^n$. Their initial pairs are $(1,1)$ and $(1,2)$, independent because the determinant is one. Thus they form a basis and every solution is uniquely $a_n=\alpha+\beta2^n$. Infinite sequence length does not imply infinite dimension when a finite number of initial freedoms determine all entries.

title: Connected difference vectors
origin: Independently reconstructed and generalized from MIT 18.06SC Problem 9.1
stem: For $n\ge2$, consider all differences $e_i-e_j$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $i<j$. Find their span, its dimension, and a basis. Then restrict differences to edges of a connected graph.
solution: Every difference has coordinate sum zero, so the span lies in the sum-zero hyperplane. The $n-1$ differences $e_i-e_n$ for $i<n$ are independent because their first $n-1$ coordinates isolate coefficients. Any sum-zero vector $x$ equals $\sum_{i<n}x_i(e_i-e_n)$, proving spanning and dimension $n-1$. If only edges of a connected graph are available, follow a path from $i$ to $n$; its signed edge differences telescope to $e_i-e_n$. Thus connected edge differences span the same space. A spanning tree supplies $n-1$ edges and hence a basis. This is a structural extension of the course exercise, not a copied assignment solution.

title: A plane, a constrained intersection, and a normal direction
origin: Independently reconstructed variation of MIT 18.06SC Problem 9.2
stem: For the plane $2x-y+4z=0$, find a basis, a basis of its intersection with $z=0$, and a basis of its perpendicular space.
solution: Solve $y=2x+4z$, giving $(x,y,z)=x(1,2,0)+z(0,4,1)$. These two generators are independent by first and third coordinates, so they are a plane basis. Imposing $z=0$ leaves the line generated by $(1,2,0)$. The vector $(2,-1,4)$ is perpendicular to both plane generators by direct dot products, each zero. The plane has dimension two in Euclidean three-space, so its perpendicular space has dimension one and that nonzero normal is a basis. The plane basis does not need to be orthogonal to serve its algebraic purpose. This variation changes the source coefficients and supplies an independently derived solution.

title: Measurement ambiguity and output dimension
origin: Original problem calibrated to Stanford EE263 range/nullspace interpretation
stem: Sensors return $y_1=x_1+x_2$ and $y_2=x_2+x_3$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$. Describe every input giving outputs $(4,7)$ and the number of independent output dimensions.
solution: Set $x_2=t$. Then $x_1=4-t$ and $x_3=7-t$, giving $(4,0,7)+t(-1,1,-1)$. The ambiguity direction is exactly the kernel of the sensor matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$. Its two rows are independent, so rank is two, nullity one, and every pair of outputs is attainable. The sensors lose one input direction rather than one of the written coordinates in isolation. A third sensor removes ambiguity only if its row is not in the span of these two rows; duplicating an existing measurement does not help.

title: Dimension of complementary projection components
stem: Let a linear map $P:V\to V$ satisfy $P^2=P$, with $V$ finite-dimensional. Prove $V=\operatorname{im}P\oplus\ker P$ without assuming orthogonality.
solution: For any $v$, write $v=Pv+(v-Pv)$. The first part is in the image; the second is in the kernel because $P(v-Pv)=Pv-P^2v=0$. Thus the two spaces span $V$. If $w=Pu$ also lies in the kernel, then $0=Pw=P^2u=Pu=w$, proving trivial intersection. The decomposition is therefore unique, and the component dimensions sum to $\dim V$. No inner product entered the proof. The projection may be oblique; idempotence alone does not imply a symmetric matrix or perpendicular components.

title: Intersection dimension from ranks of stacked constraints
stem: Let $U=\ker A$ and $W=\ker B$ in $F^n$. Derive formulas for dimensions of the intersection and sum in terms of matrix ranks.
solution: The intersection is the kernel of the vertical stack $C=\begin{bmatrix}A\\B\end{bmatrix}$, because a vector must satisfy both systems. Thus $\dim(U\cap W)=n-\operatorname{rank}C$. Separately $\dim U=n-\operatorname{rank}A$ and $\dim W=n-\operatorname{rank}B$. Substituting into the two-space dimension formula gives $\dim(U+W)=n-\operatorname{rank}A-\operatorname{rank}B+\operatorname{rank}C$. Dependencies between the two sets of constraint rows are measured by the stacked rank. For ranks two and three in $n=6$ with stacked rank four, the intersection dimension is two and the sum dimension is five.

title: A quotient of polynomial spaces
stem: In $P_4(\mathbb R)$, let $U$ be the polynomials divisible by $x^2-1$. Construct a quotient basis and an explicit coordinate formula.
solution: The subspace $U$ has basis $x^2-1,x(x^2-1),x^2(x^2-1)$ and dimension three. Polynomial division by the monic quadratic gives each polynomial a unique remainder $a+bx$. Therefore the cosets $1+U,x+U$ form a quotient basis, of dimension two. For $p=c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+c_4x^4$, reducing powers by $x^2=1$ modulo $U$ yields coordinates $(c_0+c_2+c_4,c_1+c_3)$. The remainder map is linear, its kernel is exactly $U$, and its surjectivity is clear from linear polynomials. The polynomial equality $x^2=1$ holds only in the quotient, not in the original polynomial space.

title: A hard counterexample to distributivity of subspaces
stem: Is $U\cap(W+Z)=(U\cap W)+(U\cap Z)$ always true? Establish the valid inclusion and provide a strict counterexample.
solution: A vector in the right side is a sum of two vectors both in $U$, one in $W$ and the other in $Z$. It therefore belongs to $U$ and $W+Z$, proving right-side inclusion in the left. For strictness in $\mathbb R^2$, take $U=\operatorname{span}(e_1+e_2)$, $W=\operatorname{span}e_1$, and $Z=\operatorname{span}e_2$. Then $W+Z=\mathbb R^2$, so the left side is the nonzero line $U$. Both individual intersections on the right are zero, so the right side is zero. Familiar set distributivity cannot simply be transplanted with subspace sum replacing union.

title: A valid modular identity
stem: Assume $U\subseteq Z$. Prove $U+(W\cap Z)=(U+W)\cap Z$.
solution: If $x=u+w$ with $u\in U$ and $w\in W\cap Z$, then both summands lie in $Z$ because $U\subseteq Z$. Thus $x\in(U+W)\cap Z$. Conversely let $x\in(U+W)\cap Z$, so $x=u+w$ for some $u\in U,w\in W$, and $x\in Z$. Since $u\in Z$, subtraction gives $w=x-u\in Z$. Hence $w\in W\cap Z$ and $x\in U+(W\cap Z)$. This proves equality. The containment premise is used in both directions and distinguishes this valid identity from the false unrestricted distributive identity.

title: Extending a prescribed basis using another supplied basis
stem: Let $U,W\subseteq V$ have dimensions three and three, with intersection dimension one. Can one always choose a basis of $U+W$ consisting of all three members of a prescribed basis of $U$ and two vectors from a prescribed basis of $W$? Prove your answer.
solution: Yes. The union of the prescribed basis lists spans $U+W$, whose dimension is $3+3-1=5$. Begin with all three prescribed $U$ vectors, an independent list. Process the three prescribed $W$ vectors and retain a vector exactly when it is outside the current span. Each retained vector preserves independence. At termination the retained list spans the union and hence the sum. It is therefore a five-vector basis, so exactly two $W$ vectors were retained. It is not necessarily possible to discard an arbitrarily chosen $W$ vector; the decision depends on its position relative to the current span. The constructive extension argument proves existence without assuming compatible initial bases.

title: Independent constraints on a direct sum
stem: Let $V=U\oplus W$, with dimensions four and three. Let a nonzero functional $\ell:V\to\mathbb R$ be nonzero on both $U$ and $W$. Find $\dim\ker\ell$, $\dim(U\cap\ker\ell)$, $\dim(W\cap\ker\ell)$, and determine whether these last two spaces sum to the kernel.
solution: The ambient dimension is seven. A nonzero scalar functional has rank one, so its kernel has dimension six. Its restriction to $U$ is nonzero and has rank one, so the restricted kernel has dimension three. The corresponding dimension on $W$ is two. These two restricted kernels intersect trivially because $U\cap W=0$, so their sum has dimension five. It is a proper subspace of the six-dimensional full kernel. The missing direction comes from cancellation across components: choose $u\in U$ with $\ell(u)=1$ and $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=-1$. Then $u+w\in\ker\ell$, although neither component lies in its restricted kernel. Thus a constraint on a direct sum need not split into separate zero constraints on each component.
